title: You start with an all-water grid and add land one cell at a time. After each addition, report the current number of islands. Use Union-Find with path compression and union by size.
shortTitle: Number of Islands II (Dynamic): running island count as land is added

s1_definition.oneliner: Each new land cell adds one island, then every merge with a live neighbor subtracts one: report the count after each step.
s1_definition.profdef:
Number of Islands II uses dynamic Union-Find to track island counts as land is added.

- **Union-Find** maintains disjoint sets keyed by flattened cell index (row * cols + col).
- **Land addition** increments the island count by one for each new singleton island.
- **Neighbor merge** unions the new cell with each already-land neighbor; each successful union decrements the count.
- **Duplicate addition** of an already-land cell is a no-op.
- **Path compression** and **union by size** keep the tree shallow for near-constant-time operations.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India activates banking service in map cells one at a time. Each newly activated cell starts as its own service region, raising the region count by one. If it touches an already-active neighbor, those regions fuse and the count drops. After each activation the team announces how many separate regions currently exist.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Number of Islands II is the dynamic version where land is added one cell at a time and I must report the island count after each addition. I maintain a Union-Find keyed by the flattened cell index together with a running island counter. Each time a new land cell is added, I first increment the counter because that cell is initially its own island, then I try to union it with each of its four neighbors that is already land, decrementing the counter on every union that genuinely merges two separate islands.

Using path compression with union by size keeps the trees shallow, so the whole sequence runs in time proportional to the grid plus the number of operations, each at effectively constant cost. The key operation detail is handling duplicate additions as no-ops.

At National Bank of India, a service rollout activated map cells one at a time and operations needed the current number of contiguous service regions after each activation for staffing decisions. Union-Find gave near-constant-time updates that BFS/DFS could not match.

The interviewer's favorite follow-up is land removal, and the honest answer is that plain Union-Find has no split operation. Removal is handled offline by processing the timeline in reverse and treating each removal as an addition, or by using advanced link-cut structures.

Remember one sentence: add one island per new cell, merge with live neighbors via Union-Find, decrement on each real merge, and report the count.

---

keyPoints: Union-Find tracks island counts dynamically as land is added one cell at a time
Each new land cell increments the count by one, then each neighbor merge decrements it
Path compression and union by size give near-constant-time per operation
Duplicate land additions are handled as no-ops by checking the isLand array
A single addition can merge up to 4 separate islands from all four neighbors
Standard Union-Find cannot handle land removal; use offline reverse processing as a workaround
Time is O((m*n + k) * alpha(m*n)) which is effectively O(m*n + k)
